title: Chapter II

teacherSummary.text: Victor recalls his friend Henry Clerval and his own early fascination with the alchemists Cornelius Agrippa, Paracelsus and Albertus Magnus. A lightning strike that destroys an oak tree introduces him to electricity, and he briefly turns to mathematics before 'destiny' pulls him back.

vocabulary.definition: Anything that ties or unites one thing or part to another
vocabulary.context: Thus strangely are our souls constructed, and by such slight ligaments are we bound to prosperity or ruin.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “ligament”: -ment (Latin -mentum, "result or means of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: I need not say that we were strangers to any species of disunion or dispute.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “disunion”: dis- (Latin dis-, "apart, not"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The quality or state of being loud
vocabulary.context: It advanced from behind the mountains of Jura; and the thunder burst at once with frightful loudness from various quarters of the heavens.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “loudness”: -ness (Old English -ness, "state of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: One who gives commands, or makes rules
vocabulary.context: Under the guidance of my new preceptors, I entered with the greatest diligence into the search of the philosopher’s stone and the elixir of life; but the latter soon obtained my undivided attention.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “preceptor”: pre- (Latin prae, "before") + cept (Latin capere, "to take") + -or (Latin -or, "one who"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: He might dissect, anatomise, and give names; but, not to speak of a final cause, causes in their secondary and tertiary grades were utterly unknown to him.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “dissect”: dis- (Latin dis-, "apart, not"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Her victory was announced by an unusual tranquillity and gladness of soul, which followed the relinquishing of my ancient and latterly tormenting studies.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “relinquish”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again") + quis (Latin quaerere, "to seek"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: He had partially unveiled the face of Nature, but her immortal lineaments were still a wonder and a mystery.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “unveil”: un- (Old English un-, "not"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: Incapable of being wounded, or of receiving injury
vocabulary.context: Wealth was an inferior object; but what glory would attend the discovery, if I could banish disease from the human frame, and render man invulnerable to any but a violent death!
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “invulnerable”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in") + -able (Latin -abilis, "able to be"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To split or rend into long, thin pieces
vocabulary.context: It was not splintered by the shock, but entirely reduced to thin ribbons of wood.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “splinter”: -er (Old English -ere, "one who"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Natural philosophy is the genius that has regulated my fate; I desire, therefore, in this narration, to state those facts which led to my predilection for that science.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “predilection”: pre- (Latin prae, "before") + -tion (Latin -tio, "the act of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

context.history: Agrippa and Paracelsus were Renaissance figures who mixed early science with magic. Lightning and electricity fascinated Enlightenment scientists like Benjamin Franklin.

significance: Victor frames his life as fated, shifting responsibility away from his choices—a key point for discussion.
discussionQuestions: Victor blames 'destiny' for his fate. Do you agree, or did he choose?
Where does foreshadowing appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with isolation and the need for companionship?

items.prompt: What does Victor's father call Agrippa's work?
What event introduces Victor to electricity?
Who is Victor's closest childhood friend?
What does Victor say governed his life?
In the line “Thus strangely are our souls constructed, and by such slight ligaments are we bound to prosperity or ruin.”, what does “ligaments” most nearly mean?
options: One who gives commands, or makes rules
The quality or state of being loud
Anything that ties or unites one thing or part to another

items.prompt: In the line “I need not say that we were strangers to any species of disunion or dispute.”, what does “disunion” most nearly mean?
options: The quality or state of being loud
One who gives commands, or makes rules
Anything that ties or unites one thing or part to another

answerKey.answer: Anything that ties or unites one thing or part to another

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter II,” how does Shelley show the first spark of obsession? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the foreshadowing you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter II, how does Shelley develop the idea of the first spark of obsession? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the foreshadowing in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter II develops the idea of the first spark of obsession. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of foreshadowing and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter II (where it begins, turns and ends) and its foreshadowing shape the reader's understanding of the first spark of obsession. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter II suggests about the first spark of obsession. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's foreshadowing and characterization), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Mary Shelley uses foreshadowing in Chapter II to complicate the reader's understanding of the first spark of obsession. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter II within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of the first spark of obsession responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter II alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of the first spark of obsession follows or bends those conventions, using the foreshadowing as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter II and its treatment of the first spark of obsession. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's foreshadowing and characterization, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter II as evidence for a larger claim about the first spark of obsession in Frankenstein. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter II as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of the first spark of obsession. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Frankenstein.

options: Incapable of being wounded, or of receiving injury
The quality or state of being loud
To split or rend into long, thin pieces

satQuestions.passage: The untaught peasant beheld the elements around him, and was acquainted with their practical uses. The most learned philosopher knew little more. He had partially unveiled the face of Nature, but her immortal lineaments were still a wonder and a mystery. He might dissect, anatomise, and give names; but, not to speak of a final cause, causes in their secondary and tertiary grades were utterly unknown to him. I had gazed upon the fortifications and impediments that seemed to keep human beings from entering the citadel of nature, and rashly and ignorantly I had repined.
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Chapter II”?
options: A journey and a mercenary suitor

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Victor blames 'destiny' for his fate. Do you agree, or did he choose? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are ligaments, disunion, loudness, preceptors, dissect. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “Thus strangely are our souls constructed, and by such slight ligaments are we bound to prosperity or ruin.” Webster's says: Anything that ties or unites one thing or part to another. Now the word history: “ligament”: -ment (Latin -mentum, "result or means of"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “disunion”: dis- (Latin dis-, "apart, not"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “loudness”: -ness (Old English -ness, "state of"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Frankenstein would have known. Agrippa and Paracelsus were Renaissance figures who mixed early science with magic. Lightning and electricity fascinated Enlightenment scientists like Benjamin Franklin. Why does this chapter matter? Victor frames his life as fated, shifting responsibility away from his choices—a key point for discussion. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for foreshadowing.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see foreshadowing, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to the first spark of obsession.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Foreshadowing, Characterization, Symbolism.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of foreshadowing. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: The untaught peasant beheld the elements around him, and was acquainted with their practical uses. The most learned philosopher knew little more. He had partially unveiled the face of Nature, but her immortal lineaments were still a wonder and a mystery. He might dissect, anatomise, and give names; but, not to speak of a final cause, causes in their secondary and tertiary grades were utterly unknown to him. I had gazed upon the fortifications and impediments that seemed to keep human beings from entering the citadel of nature, and rashly and ignorantly I had repined.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Foreshadowing, Characterization, Symbolism: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter II,” how does Shelley show the first spark of obsession? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the foreshadowing you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to the costs of unchecked ambition? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about the first spark of obsession, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how foreshadowing shapes the first spark of obsession. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
